title: TB0-03030
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXX (the principal claimant), her common-law partner, XXXXXXX, and the principal claimant's daughter XXXXXXXXX, all citizens of Hungary, are claiming refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The principal claimant filed an amendment to the original Personal Information Form (PIF). She was given inaccurate advice in this regard. According to the principal claimant, there are errors and omissions, therefore, she has filed the following amendment:-
The claimants fear persecution from physical atrocities as Romas at the hands of the racist Hungarians, the police, the Hungarian Guards, and the skinheads.
As well, the principal claimant fears her ex-husband, who was has been an alcoholic since 2003. According to the principal claimant, she has moved several times but it has not improved the situation.
Their fears have been exacerbated since 2007. According to the principal claimant, this is when their situation worsened and when the Death Brigades killed Roma in 2009, and they decided to flee.
With respect to the principal claimant's husband, he threatened to kill her when she divorced him. This worsened following the death of his mother.

The principal claimant describes incidents dating back to 1979 when she was excluded at a graduation party. She met her former husband, a Hungarian, in 1984. When the principal claimant became pregnant, they had to live with her parents as his family refused to have a Roma in their home. In 1987, the principal claimant was with her baby, when she was pushed off the bus by skinheads.

In 1990, the principal claimant had difficulties in building their house in a Hungarian neighbourhood. She and the children were abused. The claimants also describe difficulties in acquiring jobs and, if they did, it was for diminished pay. In 1997, the principal claimant was slapped on a bus. The bus driver refused to call the police.

The principal claimant also describes incidents when her daughter was accosted at school. She further describes an incident in 2001 when she was cursed and called names. In the summer of 2002, the principal claimant was applying for work when she and her sister were told gypsies had no place there.

In the spring of 2003, her husband began to abuse alcohol, and he began beating her, often weekly. She made as many as 15-20 reports to the police, but to no avail. On XXXXXXX, 2004 the claimants were attacked on the way to her father's funeral.

The principal claimant describes a further incident when her common-law partner and his father went fishing and a van with six men got out. Their gear was taken, and when the principal claimant's father spoke up, he was beaten

When the principal claimant told her husband in 2006 that she wanted a divorce, he attacked her with a knife. In the summer of 2008, the principal claimant's ex-husband showed up drunk, threatening to kill her and her common-law partner. Her ex-husband hit her current common-law partner with a brick. The neighbours called the police, but he was released an hour later. The local doctor treated her common-law partner. Again on XXXXXX, 2009, the principal claimant's ex-husband attacked her.

The principal claimant has suffered emotionally and indicates that her daughter was complaining of chest pains in XXXXXX 2009. They describe further incidents in XXXXX 2009 and XXXXXX 2009, when they were attacked by the Guards.
The Board finds that the principal claimant is a Convention refugee. However, we find that her daughter and common-law partner are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
The claimants' identities have been established as per the certified true copies of their passports.1 CHAIRPERSON'S GUIDELINES

The Board accepts that the principal claimant was abused over a period of approximately six years. We have, therefore, considered the gender guidelines2 before arriving at our decision. The Board also took into account the lack of education, and lack of sophistication when interpreting the principal claimant's responses.

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The principles, enunciated hereafter, pertain to the case at hand and were accordingly applied. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.4

Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection does not mean that the state on the whole fails to protect its citizens, unless those failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.5 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on the claimant to approach other members of the security forces or the authorities.6

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.7 The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.8 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.9

While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration,10 the preponderance of recent Federal Court decisions has held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than effective per se.11 A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken, and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.12

The Board must consider what steps the principal claimant took to seek state protection. She fears the racists in Hungary as well as her former husband. It is her former husband, which leads the Board to conclude that her fears are well-founded.

According to the claimant's testimony, she went to the police between 20 and 40 occasions. She also went to two different locations to obtain restraining orders without success. She also asked her sister to obtain additional copies of police reports without success.13 She further alleges that she consulted with the Roma Self-Government.14
The principal claimant testified that her former husband was very resentful when he was denied an inheritance from his family when his mother died. He was denied this because he married a Roma.

The principal claimant separated from her former husband in 2007 and was divorced on XXXXXX, 2008. However, he threatened her many times subsequently, and after she had met her current common-law partner.
Although at times, the police attended, the perpetrator received a fine on only one occasion and no other penalty.

The Board concludes that the principal claimant has rebutted the presumption of state protection. We have no reason to disbelieve her testimony regarding her attempts to seek state protection. Moreover, it was corroborated by her daughter, who, not only witnessed some of the abuse, but actually went to the police with her.

Documentary evidence indicates that Hungary is a republic with a population of approximately 10 million and a multiparty parliamentary democracy. Legislative authority is vested in the unicameral parliament (National Assembly). The elections held in 2006 were assessed as free and fair. Civilian authorities generally maintained effective control of the security forces.

The constitution and law prohibit arbitrary arrest and detention, and the government generally observed these prohibitions. According to the Prosecutor General's Office, there were 65 official complaints of arbitrary detention. The Prosecutor General's office rejected 22 complaints and initiated indictments in three cases.

The Hungarian National Police (HNP), which operates under the direction of the Ministry of Justice and Law Enforcement, is responsible for enforcing laws and maintaining order nationwide. Twenty regional police departments are directly subordinate to the HNP; city police are subordinate to the regional police and have local jurisdiction: the Republican Guard; the National Bureau of Investigation; and the Emergency Police, which are also responsible for counterterrorism and crowd control.

Corruption within police agencies remained a problem. Penalties for police officers found guilty of wrongdoing include reprimand, dismissal, and criminal prosecution. The Independent Police Complaints Board (IPCB), established in 2008, continued to investigate violations and omissions by the police that substantively concerned fundamental rights. The five-member body, appointed by a two-thirds majority of the National Assembly, functions independently of police authorities.15

With respect to domestic violence, while the Hungarian Penal Code does not contain any sections that deal exclusively with the problem of domestic violence, it does criminalize actions which constitute domestic violence. The general charge of assault and battery, which carries a maximum prison term of eight years, is used to prosecute domestic violence cases. Hungary has ratified the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), as well as the Convention's Optional Protocol.16 The Federal Court17 has stated that the Board: ... may also assume that a country adhering to an international convention will meet its obligation to implement the convention within its own territory if that be required, unless evidence to the contrary is adduced.

The Board's documents state that domestic abuse or violence is a common and serious problem in Hungary, with approximately one in five women threatened with or victimized by domestic violence.18 The majority of Hungarian women do not report the abuse. However, the test in refugee cases is forward looking. As Justice Pratte stated in Mileva:19 ...The question raised by a claim to refugee status is not whether the claimants had reason to fear persecution in the past, but rather whether he now, at the time his claim is being decided, has good grounds to fear persecution in the future.

Therefore, it is not enough to examine Hungary's historical record on domestic violence or traditional social norms. It is necessary to look at the current efforts being undertaken by the Hungarian state to protect victims of domestic abuse. The Board's documents indicate that Hungary has taken a number of measures to deal with domestic violence.20 On 1 July 2006, a law on restraining orders came into effect. The Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour launched a separate website on domestic violence, continued to operate a 24-hour hotline for victims of domestic abuse, and increased the number of government-run shelters for abused women from seven to 10. The Hungarian Ministry of Youth, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities operates a 24-hour hotline for victims of domestic violence.

However, domestic violence remains a great problem in Hungary. According to the latest study, at least a million women have been victims of marital violence and annually between 50 and 150 women are killed by a member of their families, which represents more than one woman homicide victim per week. The official data are incomplete, however, the Criminal Code does not define domestic violence as a major or serious offence. Consequently, police and prosecution-service major crime figures cannot take domestic violence into account. In response to this situation, the police are starting to receive training from NGOs and international organizations in dealing with domestic violence and are beginning to treat it as an offence rather than a matter for the individual couple. However, the absence of specific penalties for acts of domestic violence does not make it any easier for the police and courts to deal with it. There are further problems regarding victims' complaints and confidentiality of the procedure. Perpetrators mostly receive mere fines or suspended sentences. According to the authorities, when life is threatened, the Court's ruling must include a sentence of imprisonment. Furthermore, a 2005 amendment to the Criminal Code allows a judge or the prosecutor to order a person on probation to keep away from a victim, his/her home or workplace. Hungary does not yet have a network of shelters for battered women that is adequate to the problem. At present the Budapest shelter run by the Salvation Army and which can accommodate 20 people or three families is the only facility solely for victims of domestic violence and their children. For lack of any other specialist facilities, victims are forced to take refuge in the 90 hostels for women and families in distress. These are a last resort and do not fully meet victims' needs. Firstly, their addresses are not kept secret. Secondly they are not always equipped to accommodate children (the very young, and the older teenager), women with handicaps or children with handicaps. Lastly the staff are not always trained to protect and support victims of violence or appropriate or adequately qualified for that task. To remedy this unacceptable gap in provision, the Ministry of Youth, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities launched a program in the second half of 2005 with the aim of opening four facilities in each county and four in Budapest for women victims of domestic violence and their children. Several associations and NGOs have responded to the government call for tenders. This program, which is extremely welcome and deserves support, has experienced, and continues to experience, certain financial difficulties. According to information provided by Hungarian authorities, 8 temporary family homes have been chosen to provide accommodation and complex help to the victims fleeing from domestic abuse with or without children. The opening of a secret shelter is foreseen and will exclusively accommodate women victims of domestic violence with or without children. Lastly, the Hungarian authorities have for several years been discussing the possibility of enacting domestic-violence legislation. In 2003 Parliament adopted a resolution on development of a national strategy to prevent and fight domestic violence. This resolution stated that domestic violence cannot and should not be considered as a private matter. As a result the Ministry of the Interior issued regulatory measures to step up police action on the question and to adopt a victim-oriented approach. In a 2005 Resolution, the Government instructed its different bodies to develop the training of experts in the field of domestic violence. Although the law provides for restraining orders, such orders can be imposed only in specific circumstances and only for a maximum of 30 days. According to the Open Society Institute, the restraining order in its present form does not provide effective protection for victims; in fact, it adds virtually nothing to previous legal possibilities. The OSI reports that there is no national coordinating body to address violence against women. However, according to the Hungarian government, the Working Group on Violence Against Women established in 2007 coordinates joint efforts by various government ministries and law enforcement bodies to prevent domestic violence. However, the lack of social, psychological and legal support available to female victims of domestic violence in Hungary has been criticized. Country Reports notes that many NGOs characterize Hungarian state efforts to protect victims of domestic violence as insufficient. Amnesty International indicates that a parliamentary resolution to combat domestic violence, passed in 2003 following public pressure, "remained largely unimplemented".

With respect to the principal claimant, we find that she made reasonable efforts in her particular circumstances to seek state protection. Although there were some contradictory statements, the Board took into account the lack of sophistication of the principal claimant along with her fragile emotional state.

We also considered the viability of an internal flight alternative. However, in her particular circumstances, we find that she sought protection in several locations without success. We found the corroborative evidence while in some instances self-serving, sufficient to validate an objective basis for her claim, particularly her young daughter's testimony, which we found to be compelling.
Accordingly, we find the principal claimant to be a Convention refugee. ANALYSIS RE: DAUGHTER

Although the principal claimant's daughter, XXXXXX, observed a number of the beatings her mother received at the hands of her father, she, herself was not abused. We accept that she was undoubtedly emotionally affected by this, however there was no evidence adduced to persuade the Board that she would have a well-founded fear of her father, if she were to return to Hungary. On the contrary, sadly, it appeared that her father, given the evidence that he had made no contact with the claimant since her parents' divorce, did not wish to maintain a relationship with her.

Although the principal claimant describes a few incidents relating to racism at the hands of the Hungarian guards, there was no evidence adduced to persuade the Board that this was tantamount to persecution. The narrative of the principal claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) describes incidents during XXXXXX school years, however, for the most part, her PIF relates to racism targeted at the principal claimant and not her daughter. ANALYSIS RE: COMMON-LAW PARTNER

This claimant alleges he, too, fears the principal claimant's former husband. He described one incident when her former husband hit him with a brick. He also described an incident which occurred in XXXXXX 2008 when he was threatened by a Hungarian guard. There was no persuasive evidence that this claimant had suffered harm at the hands of either the principal claimant's former husband, or at the hands of the Hungarian Guards, which would be tantamount to persecution.
Moreover, there was no persuasive evidence that this claimant had rebutted the presumption of state protection.

Accordingly, the Board finds that the principal claimant is a Convention refugee. Her common-law partner and her daughter's claims are rejected.
